sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard institutional systems: learning management systems, student information systems, gradebooks, and document repositories. AI components are usually deployed as plugins or batch processes that read exported course data, syllabi, and assessment rubrics. No special hardware is required beyond typical cloud or on-premises servers. The site's catalogue of 805 scientific models and 732 AI tools indexes the specific implementations referenced in the research, but this page does not endorse any single vendor.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners typically extract learning outcome statements from course documents using natural language processing, then classify them against taxonomies such as Bloom's or SOLO. They align outcomes to assessment items and learning activities by measuring semantic similarity or by rule-based mapping. Some workflows cluster related outcomes across a programme to find gaps or redundancies. The output is usually a revised outcome map or a set of alignment reports for course teams.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Student data used for outcome prediction or curriculum analytics is subject to institutional privacy rules and, in many jurisdictions, specific education records law. Risks include biased predictions about learner progress, over-reliance on automated alignment scores, and loss of provenance when outcome statements are rewritten by generative models. Course teams should keep a record of which model version produced which recommendation and which training data informed it. The site's library links to original papers so that readers can check the evidence behind any claim, rather than relying on a secondary search tool.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of work is toward continuous curriculum review, where outcome data updates each term rather than during periodic programme reviews. Generative models are being tested for drafting outcome statements and suggesting assessment alignments, but human review remains the norm. Competency-based and microcredential programmes are pushing for finer-grained outcome tracking across courses and institutions. The site's catalogue of 91 AI books and 805 scientific models will continue to grow as this area matures.
